name: The Doctrine of Double Effect
statement: It can be permissible to cause a harm as a foreseen side effect that would be wrong to cause as a means.
statementAccent: as a foreseen side effect that would be wrong to cause as a means
meaning: The doctrine of double effect, also called the principle of double effect, is a set of ethical criteria for judging the permissibility of an action that will produce both a good effect and a serious harm. Its core claim is that it can be permissible to cause a harm as a merely foreseen side effect of pursuing a good end, even when it would not be permissible to cause that same harm as a means to the good end, or to intend it. The doctrine is traditionally traced to the thirteenth-century philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas, who discussed it in his Summa Theologica in the context of killing an assailant in self-defense, noting that a single act can have two effects, only one of which is intended. The doctrine turns on the distinction between intending a harm and merely foreseeing it, and between causing a harm as a means and causing it as a side effect. It is standardly stated in four conditions: the act itself must be morally good or neutral; the agent must intend only the good effect, with the bad effect foreseen but not intended; the good effect must not be produced by means of the bad effect; and there must be a proportionately grave reason for permitting the harm. The doctrine is influential in medical ethics, just war theory, and Catholic moral theology.
mechanism: The doctrine of double effect works by making the permissibility of causing a harm depend not only on the harm itself but on the agent's intention and on the causal structure of the act. Its four traditional conditions must all be met. First, the act performed must be, in itself, morally good or at least morally neutral, not intrinsically wrong. Second, the agent must intend only the good effect; the bad effect may be foreseen and tolerated but must not be part of what the agent aims at. Third, and crucially, the good effect must not be brought about by means of the bad effect, so that the harm is a side effect of achieving the good, not the mechanism through which the good is achieved. Fourth, there must be a proportionately grave reason for permitting the harm, weighing the good sought against the harm caused. The two key distinctions doing the work are between intending a harm and merely foreseeing it, and between harm caused as a means and harm caused as a side effect. Thus the doctrine can permit an act with a bad effect that is foreseen but unintended and not used as a means, while forbidding an otherwise similar act in which the same harm is intended or serves as the means to the good.

examples.text: Giving a dying patient enough morphine to relieve pain, foreseeing but not intending that it may hasten death, can be permissible.
Killing civilians to break enemy morale is impermissible, but bombing a military target while foreseeing civilian deaths may be permitted.
Diverting a trolley so one dies as a side effect may be permitted, while pushing a person to their death as the means to stop it is not.

variants.name: The four conditions
variants.text: That the act is good or neutral, the harm is not intended, the harm is not the means, and there is proportionate reason.

variants.name: Intend versus foresee
variants.text: The central distinction between intending a harm and merely foreseeing it as an unintended side effect.

whyItMatters: The doctrine of double effect is one of the most influential principles in applied ethics, providing a widely used framework for thinking about situations in which doing good unavoidably brings about harm. By distinguishing between harm that is intended or used as a means and harm that is merely foreseen as a side effect, the doctrine captures a deep and common moral intuition, that there is a moral difference between aiming at a harm and permitting it in the course of pursuing a good, an intuition that pure consequentialism cannot easily accommodate. This makes the doctrine central to medical ethics, where it governs cases like the use of pain-relieving drugs that may hasten death, and to just war theory, where it distinguishes deliberately targeting civilians from foreseeably harming them while striking military targets. It has deep roots in Catholic moral theology and continues to structure debates about euthanasia, abortion, and the ethics of killing. The doctrine also connects to major puzzles in moral philosophy, including the trolley problem, and to the broader question of whether and how intention bears on the permissibility of action.

limits: The doctrine of double effect is powerful but faces serious criticisms. The closeness problem holds that it is often hard to distinguish a harm that is genuinely a foreseen side effect from one so tightly bound to the chosen means that it is effectively intended, as in disputed cases where a fetal death seems both means and side effect depending on how the act is described. A deeper objection questions whether an agent's intention is even relevant to the permissibility of an action: consequentialists deny that it is, holding that what matters is the outcome, not the mental state, and some non-consequentialists argue that intention bears on the assessment of the agent or their character rather than on whether the act itself is permissible. There is also persistent difficulty in defining intention precisely and in specifying what is intended as a means versus merely foreseen.
misreadings: The doctrine of double effect does not say any harm is permitted so long as one has good intentions; all four conditions must be met, including that the harm not be the means and that there be proportionate reason. It does not permit intending harm, only foreseeing it as an unintended side effect. And it is not uncontroversial, since the closeness problem and the question of whether intention affects permissibility are serious challenges, so treating the doctrine as excusing any harm with good intent, as allowing intended harm, or as beyond dispute, misreads a carefully conditioned and contested principle.
origin: A set of ethical criteria traditionally traced to Thomas Aquinas's thirteenth-century discussion of self-defense, holding that harm may be permissible as a foreseen side effect but not as an intended means; central to medical ethics and just war theory.
